segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I praise you because you remember me in everything and hold fast to the traditions just as I handed them on to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of a woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Every man who prays or prophesies with something down over his head shames his head;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered shames her head, for she is one and the same as the woman who has been shaved.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if a woman does not cover herself, let her have her hair cut off as well; but if it is shameful for a woman to have her hair cut off or to be shaved, let her cover herself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For man is not from woman, but woman from man;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and indeed man was not created for the sake of the woman, but woman for the sake of the man.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason the woman ought to have authority over her head, because of the angels.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nevertheless, in the Lord neither is woman apart from man nor man apart from woman.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For just as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman; and all things are from God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judge for yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God uncovered?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair, it is a dishonor to him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but if a woman wears long hair, it is her glory? For long hair has been given as a wrap.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor do the assemblies of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But in giving this instruction I do not praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in the first place, when you come together as an assembly, I hear that there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For there must indeed be factions among you, so that those who stand the test may become evident among you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when you come together in one place, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for in the eating each one goes ahead with his own supper, and one goes hungry while another gets drunk.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the assembly of God and shame those who have nothing? What should I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was being handed over, took bread,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and after giving thanks he broke it and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way he took the cup also, after the supper, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be answerable for the body and the blood of the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let a person test themselves, and so eat from the bread and drink from the cup;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the one who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a good number have fallen asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if we were discerning ourselves, we would not be judged;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: yet when we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined, so that we may not be condemned along with the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, my brothers and sisters, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment. The remaining matters I will set in order when I come.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary word for the physical head, and Paul plays on the literal and figurative senses throughout verses 3–10. What the figure means is disputed: the majority view is that it signals authority or pre-eminence, while a substantial minority argue for 'source' or 'origin', pointing to verses 8 and 12. The translation keeps 'head' so that the wordplay stays visible and the question stays open.

Greek uses the same words for 'man' and 'husband' and for 'woman' and 'wife'. Some translations render this clause 'the head of a wife is her husband' and read the whole passage as being about married couples. The appeal to creation in verses 8–9 and 12 suits the broader 'man' and 'woman', which is used here throughout, but the narrower sense cannot be ruled out.

notes.phrase: with something down over his head
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'having down from the head' and does not name what hangs down. Most interpreters take it as a cloth covering, such as the fold of the toga that Roman men drew over the head when offering sacrifice. Others, noting verses 14–15, take it as long hair worn loose. The rendering leaves the object unstated, as the Greek does.

notes.traditional: have a symbol of authority on her head
notes.note: The Greek says only 'have authority over [or on] the head'; the words 'a symbol of' are supplied by most translations, on the view that the covering is a sign of the authority she is under. Elsewhere, though, 'to have authority over' something means to exercise control over it, which would make the woman the one who holds authority over her own head. Both readings have serious scholarly support, and the plain wording of the Greek is kept here.

Paul does not explain this phrase and its meaning is uncertain. The most common suggestion is that angels were thought to be present at the community's worship and to watch over its good order, an idea found in Jewish texts of the period. Others see a reference to the angels of Genesis 6 who desired human women, or take the word in its other sense of human 'messengers' visiting from elsewhere.

The noun means a garment wrapped around the body, and is a different word from the 'cover' and 'uncovered' of verses 5–13. The preposition can mean 'as, answering to' or 'instead of'. On the second reading a woman's long hair takes the place of a garment, which some scholars use to argue that the whole passage concerns hairstyle rather than a veil. Most take it in the first sense, as an argument from nature supporting a covering.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city's citizen assembly, or, in the Greek Old Testament, Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation to keep the first-century sense.

It is not clear which custom is meant. It may be the practice Paul has been arguing against (women praying uncovered), which is why some translations paraphrase as 'no other practice'. It may instead be the custom of being contentious. The Greek word means 'such', not 'other', and is translated accordingly.

At this period the Lord's supper was part of a full shared meal, usually in a wealthier member's house. The verb normally means to take or do something beforehand, suggesting that those with leisure and food began before poorer members arrived; this fits 'wait for one another' in verse 33. Some scholars argue that it means simply 'consumes', so that the fault is eating one's own food without sharing rather than eating early.

Most translations have 'betrayed', referring to Judas, and that may be what is in view. But the verb is the ordinary word for handing over, the same one translated 'handed on' earlier in this verse, and Paul elsewhere uses it of God giving up his Son and of Christ giving himself up (Romans 8:32; Galatians 2:20). 'Handed over' keeps the repetition and leaves room for the wider sense.

The earliest manuscripts read simply 'which is for you'. Later copies add 'broken' (or in a few cases 'given'), and many also add 'Take, eat' before 'This is my body'; these readings underlie the King James Version. They are generally regarded as expansions influenced by the Gospel accounts and by liturgical use.

'The body' may be the body of Christ signified by the bread, or the community as Christ's body (as in 10:17 and chapter 12), which the Corinthians were dishonoring by humiliating their poorer members; many scholars think both are in play. Later manuscripts add 'unworthily' and 'of the Lord', which narrows the sense to the first. Verses 29–34 play on a single Greek root, reflected here in 'judgment', 'discerning', 'judged' and 'condemned'.

Everywhere else in the New Testament this verb means 'wait for', and that is the majority rendering here. Outside the New Testament it can also mean 'receive' or 'welcome', and some scholars prefer 'welcome one another', that is, share the meal as hosts rather than merely delay it.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs in every letter, and translations split between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'friends'; it needs one policy.
The traditional 'betray' for Jesus's handing over hides the link with the same verb used of God, of Jesus himself and of the passing on of tradition, across the Gospels and the letters.
The choice between 'woman' and 'wife' (and 'man' and 'husband' for ἀνήρ) changes the meaning of several disputed passages in the letters and should follow a stated rule.
The word means 'covenant' in Septuagint usage but 'will' or 'testament' in ordinary Greek, and Galatians 3 and Hebrews 9 exploit both senses, so the rendering needs a consistent rule.
The figurative sense (authority or source) is disputed here and in Ephesians and Colossians, and readers should see the same English word in each place.
